analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for workers to unionize and bargain by weakening employer tools to block them.
analysis.headline: The Workplace Democracy Act was introduced in May 2018 and died in the Senate committee it was referred to, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal labor law to make union organizing much easier. Workers could form a union by signing authorization cards (with no employer-forced secret election), employers would have to start bargaining within 10 days of certification, and stalled first contracts would go to binding arbitration. It would also crack down on employer tactics: workers could not be labeled "independent contractors" or "supervisors" to keep them out of unions, companies using temp or subcontracted workers would share legal liability for labor violations, states could no longer bar mandatory union dues ("right to work" laws), and employers and their anti-union consultants would face new disclosure and registration requirements with penalties up to $10,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want a union, especially in industries where employers currently stall, misclassify, or litigate organizing campaigns to death: warehouse, retail, fast food, delivery, and temp agency workers. Workers who already benefit from union contracts but live in right-to-work states would gain, since unions could collect dues from everyone the contract covers, giving unions more resources to represent and organize.

how_it_helps.text: Allows the National Labor Relations Board to certify a union without a secret-ballot election whenever a majority of eligible workers have signed valid authorization cards, shortening a process employers can currently stretch out for months [S2][S3].

Requires employers to begin bargaining with a newly certified union within 10 days, and if no first contract is reached after mediation fails, a binding arbitration board settles the dispute for two years — ending the common tactic of refusing to reach a first contract indefinitely [S2][S3].

Stops employers from dodging union law by classifying workers as independent contractors or supervisors: a worker is an employee unless truly in business for themselves and outside the employer's usual business [S2][S3].

Makes companies that set the terms of employment for temp agency or subcontracted workers jointly and severally liable for labor law violations, so lead companies can no longer hide behind a staffing intermediary [S3].

Repeals the section of federal law that lets states prohibit requiring union dues from workers covered by union contracts, overriding right-to-work laws in the more than half of states that have them [S2][S3].

Requires employers to report payments to anti-union consultants within 7 days (24 hours before an election), register and certify those consultants, and disclose negative anti-union information sent to employees, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation [S3].
Prohibits coercing employees into attending anti-union campaign activities and lifts legal restrictions on secondary boycotts and picketing, restoring tools unions lost in 1947 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially large ones with nonunion workforces and high union-avoidance spending. They would face faster, harder-to-block organizing, shared liability for staffing agency workers, possible binding first contracts set by an arbitrator, mandatory reporting of anti-union spending, and in right-to-work states, contracts requiring dues from all covered employees. Some of these costs could show up in consumer prices or in pressure on hiring.

drawbacks.text: Replacing the secret-ballot election with card-sign certification removes the private voting booth; opponents argue workers could be pressured to sign cards by union organizers in ways a private election would prevent [S2].

Government-imposed binding arbitration of first contracts means a three-person board can set wages, benefits, and work rules for two years if bargaining stalls — a significant expansion of government-set labor terms that employers would bear [S3].
Repealing right-to-work provisions means workers who decline to join the union could still be legally required to pay dues or fees as a condition of employment [S2].

The broader definition of employee and joint-employer liability would sweep many genuine independent contractors and franchise arrangements into union coverage, which small businesses argued would raise their costs and complicate contracting [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who want collective bargaining, the benefits are large and direct: the bill removes nearly every procedural lever employers use to slow or defeat organizing, and it puts teeth into first contracts through arbitration. The costs fall mostly on employers, some of which would be passed to consumers or absorbed in hiring. The real trade-offs are on process — card-sign certification trades the privacy of a ballot box for speed, and mandatory dues trade individual choice for union funding. Whether those trade-offs are acceptable is genuinely contested; what is not contested is that the bill would shift power decisively from employers to organized labor.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and the Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the Workplace Democracy Act in the Senate on May 9, 2018, joined by 12 other senators as original sponsors [S1][S3].
The bill's only action beyond introduction was being read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large nonunion employers and the union-avoidance consulting industry, who would have faced faster organizing, joint liability, and mandatory disclosure of anti-union spending. Right-to-work states also kept their existing law. Workers gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Workplace Democracy Act in the Senate and recruited 12 original cosponsors.

for.name: Democratic senators (Gillibrand, Warren, Brown, Baldwin, Whitehouse, Harris, Merkley, Markey, Booker, Wyden, Leahy, Van Hollen)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors the day the bill was introduced; 16 Democratic senators cosponsored in total.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, took no recorded action on it — no hearing or markup was ever scheduled.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; as majority leader he controlled what legislation received floor time.

against.name: Employer and business groups (e.g., U.S. Chamber of Commerce)
against.what_they_did: Opposed card-sign union certification, mandatory-dues contracts, and joint-employer liability, which were top legislative priorities for organized business in this era.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors were Democrats or the one Independent who caucuses with them; no Republican supported the bill, and the Republican-controlled committee and floor never gave it a vote.

industries.industry: Large nonunion employers (retail, fast food, logistics, warehousing)
industries.note: These companies currently rely on long election timelines, contractor and supervisor classifications, and staffing intermediaries to keep workforces nonunion. The bill removes those levers and adds joint liability and mandatory anti-union spending disclosure, so their interest runs against the workers seeking to organize them.

industries.industry: Union-avoidance consultants and labor relations firms
industries.note: An industry built on advising employers how to defeat organizing drives would face registration, criminal background checks, 7-day payment disclosures, and per-day penalties. Their business model depends on operating without the visibility this bill requires.

industries.industry: Temp and staffing agencies and lead companies that use them
industries.note: Joint and several liability means the companies that actually set working conditions can no longer shift labor law liability to a staffing intermediary.

The bill's new employee definition makes it far harder to classify workers as independent contractors, directly threatening the contractor-based business model of delivery and rideshare platforms. Workers on those platforms would gain union rights they currently lack.

Unions would gain a much easier certification path, mandatory bargaining timelines, arbitration for first contracts, repeal of right-to-work restrictions on dues, and restored secondary boycott rights — more members, more resources, and more leverage.
